title: Poached Eggs
subtitle: The technique for perfectly set whites and a runny yolk
excerpt: The most technique-dependent of all egg preparations. Fresh eggs, barely simmering water, and a vinegar splash are the only things between you and a tidy, cloud-like result.
sourceNotes: Classic French technique adopted across British cooking. The vinegar method for coagulating egg white quickly is well-established in British cooking schools and home cookery literature.

glossaryTerms.definition: To cook food gently submerged in liquid held just below simmering point, around 80 to 90 °C. The liquid should show occasional lazy bubbles, not a rolling boil.
To heat liquid to a temperature just below boiling, around 85 to 95 °C, so that small bubbles rise steadily to the surface but the liquid does not roll or churn.

content.text: A poached egg is one of the purest tests of technique in the breakfast kitchen. The ideal version has a fully set white with no raw, snotty patches and a yolk that is warm and runny, firm enough to hold when you lift it, liquid enough to burst over toast. Getting there consistently comes down to three things: using the freshest eggs you can find, keeping the water at the right temperature, and not rushing it.
What you need

content.text: Set up the water
Half-fill the saucepan with water and bring it to a gentle
simmer

over medium heat. You want small bubbles rising slowly, not a rolling boil. Add the white wine vinegar. It helps the egg white coagulate quickly so the egg holds its shape instead of spreading into threads through the water.

While the water heats, crack each egg individually into a small cup or ramekin. Do not crack them straight into the pan, a single broken yolk ruins the batch. Crack them one by one into the cup and check each before it goes near the water.
The vortex method

Stir the simmering water in a circular motion with a spoon to create a gentle vortex. Slide one egg from its cup into the centre of the swirl. The spinning water wraps the white around the yolk, encouraging a neater shape. Cook for 3 minutes for a runny yolk, 3.5 minutes for a slightly more set yolk, or 4 minutes for a yolk that is just starting to firm at the edges but still soft in the middle.
When cooking multiple eggs, you can add them one at a time at 30-second intervals. Keep the water at a gentle
poach
throughout, if it starts to boil, the whites will tear and the eggs will bounce around the pan. Reduce the heat if needed.
Lift and serve

Lift each egg out with a slotted spoon and let it drain over the pan for a few seconds. You can rest the spoon briefly on a clean folded tea towel to absorb any remaining water before it goes on toast. Season with a pinch of sea salt and a grind of pepper. Serve immediately, a poached egg waits for no one.

For a dinner party or batch situation, poach the eggs a few minutes early and lower them into a bowl of cold water to stop the cooking. When you are ready to serve, drop them back into hot (not boiling) water for 30 to 60 seconds to reheat.
Timing reference
These timings assume a fresh large egg dropped into gently simmering water at around 90 °C. Very cold eggs from the fridge need an extra 30 to 45 seconds.
3 minutes: fully runny yolk, white just set at the edges but possibly still a little soft on top
3 minutes 30 seconds: runny yolk, white fully set all round
4 minutes: yolk starting to set at the very outside, still liquid in the centre
Troubleshooter

White spreading into threads: the egg is not fresh enough, or the water is too cold and the white is setting too slowly. Fresh eggs have tighter whites that cling to the yolk. Old eggs have looser whites that drift. The vinegar helps but won't rescue an egg that is a week old.

Yolk broken before cooking: the yolk membrane weakens as eggs age. Crack gently, tap once on the rim of the bowl rather than the pan edge, then pull the shell apart cleanly. A flat surface gives you more control than a sharp edge.

Eggs sticking to the pan base: the water temperature has dropped too low. Keep the heat steady. Eggs should never sit on the bottom; they should float in the water column. If they settle, gently nudge them with the slotted spoon.
Where this dish lives

The poached egg is central to some of Britain's best-loved breakfast and brunch dishes, eggs Benedict, eggs Florentine, eggs Royale, and appears on avocado toast menus from Shoreditch to Bath. The technique is French in origin but has been thoroughly absorbed into British breakfast culture. A well-made poached egg on brown toast with a pinch of sea salt is one of those things that needs nothing else.
